meta.title: Latchwire — WireGuard® compatible client with the key on your YubiKey
meta.desc: Open-source, WireGuard® compatible client that keeps the private key inside a YubiKey. Pre-release: command line for macOS and Linux.
og.line: Open source · WireGuard® compatible · The private key stays on your YubiKey
draft.note: This translation is an unreviewed draft. If it differs from the English page, the English page is right.
hero.h1: Make your VPN key impossible to copy.
hero.sub: Latchwire keeps your WireGuard private key inside a YubiKey. The key is generated on the card and never leaves it. The protocol and your server stay the same. No card, no tunnel.
hero.status: Pre-release: command line for macOS and Linux
how.s1h: Generate the key on your YubiKey
how.s1p: Run keygen with a YubiKey on firmware {firmware} or later. The key is created on the card, in a retired PIV slot ({slotFirst}–{slotLast}), and other slots stay as they are. A card with factory settings gets a new PIN and PUK first.
how.s2h: Add the public key to your server
how.s2p: Your server sees an ordinary WireGuard peer, so it needs no plugin or update. Latchwire is built for standard servers such as OPNsense, pfSense, Linux and MikroTik. So far it has been tested end to end only against a test server in a Linux container.
how.s3p: The PIN goes to the card and is not stored. You normally enter it once; it is asked again after sleep or when another program resets the card. Remove the card and the tunnel comes down. The target is two seconds; a test with a simulated card took about one.
cmp.r1a: In a file on your computer
cmp.r2b: No. The key cannot be taken off the card
cmp.r3a: Replace the key on every server
cmp.r3b: Nothing on the disk can complete a handshake
cmp.r4a: It can steal the key and use it later
cmp.r4b: It can use the tunnel while the card is plugged in, but it cannot take the key away
cmp.r5b: A second YubiKey, added to the server as a second peer
hw.lead: Only the first card below exists in code today. The labels say what each one is.
hw.c1p: PIV with X25519, firmware {firmware} or later. The key is generated on the card and never leaves it. Tests so far use simulated cards; checks on real cards are still open.
hw.c2p: Planned right after v1. Not implemented.
hw.c3p: Planned right after v1, for devices with X25519. Not implemented.
hw.c4p: Weaker class, not in v1. The key would be encrypted by hardware but exposed in memory while in use, so these will never carry the claim that the key cannot be copied.
sec.lead: The claim is about taking the key, not about using it. Here is what that covers and what it does not.
sec.y1: Copying the key from your disk or backups: no private key is ever written there
sec.y2: A stolen or imaged laptop without the card
sec.y3: Configuration files that carry a private key: Latchwire rejects them
sec.y4: Keys that were not generated on the card: Latchwire refuses them
sec.y5: Traffic leaving outside the tunnel while the kill switch is on, within the limits in the threat model
sec.n1: Malware running as you while the card is plugged in and the PIN is entered: it can use the card and the tunnel. No touch is required
sec.n2: Other programs that can reach the card after the PIN is entered; on some systems this includes other local users
sec.n3: A compromised root account or kernel
sec.n4: A stolen laptop together with the card and the PIN
sec.n5: Reading process memory: session keys and a cached secret live there and can reach swap. They are not the private key, and they cannot complete a handshake without the card
sec.n6: Counterfeit tokens: Latchwire trusts what the card reports and does not check attestation yet
sec.note1: The PIN is never stored, but it passes through memory while you type it.
sec.note2: The default PIN is never tried.
sec.note3: A preshared key, if you use one, is stored on disk and is not protected by hardware.
sec.note4: The threat model names the code behind each protection. If the two disagree, the code is right and the document has a bug.
st.lead: Latchwire is pre-release software. This is what exists today and what has been checked.
st.r1p: Tested end to end in a privileged container, with a software key and a test server.
st.r2p: Implemented. The manual checks are still open.
st.r3p: Automated tests use simulated cards. The checks on real cards are still open.
st.r4p: Not implemented. The Windows build does not compile yet.
st.r5p: In development. Today there is only the command line.
st.r6p: There are no releases. You build from source.
st.r7p: There has been no independent review.
inst.lead: Build from source. There are no packages or signed binaries yet, and this setup is for testing.
inst.req: You need Go {go} or later and a YubiKey 5 with firmware {firmware} or later. On Linux you also need a C compiler and libpcsclite-dev to build, and a running pcscd.
inst.s2: Start the daemon and the agent, each in its own terminal
inst.s3p: keygen prints a [Peer] block for your server. Your tunnel file is a normal WireGuard file with KeyRef and PublicKey in place of PrivateKey.
inst.pkg: Homebrew, .deb, .rpm and Microsoft Store packages are planned. None of them exists yet.
road.r1p: Command-line client for macOS and Linux
road.r2p: Full tunnel, DNS, kill switch, on-demand and allowed users. Tested on Linux; macOS still to be checked
road.r3p: Real YubiKeys and macOS networking, using the public checklist
road.r4p: Service, network layer and kill switch
road.r5p: Desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux
